prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize for topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After the first round the scientific case looks stronger to me, not weaker, because no colleague disputes it. Every member who criticised B024 did so on attribution, and none on soundness or maturity. The mechanism is the kind I trust: a bulk Z2 invariant, defined for a band structure independent of microscopic detail, forces protected boundary states, and this was predicted in 2005 by Kane and Mele, tested quantitatively in 2007 by Molenkamp's group (edge conductance close to 2e^2/h in HgTe wells), and then confirmed by ARPES, STM and transport on several independent material platforms. Fifteen to twenty years of independent confirmation gives a stable interpretation, which answers the maturity question that sinks B013 for me. On Mele versus Hasan I have now looked at the credit more carefully. The Kane-Mele papers introduced both the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall idea, and the three-dimensional generalisation was also worked out by Kane and Mele together with Fu, so a theory pair covers the 2D and 3D conceptual content. Dropping Mele would split a founding pair on the strength of the three-person cap alone. Hasan's ARPES observation is a real experimental milestone, but it confirms a prediction that the theory had already made, whereas Molenkamp's experiment is the first observation of the effect itself. I therefore keep Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and word the citation around the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator so that it does not claim to credit the 3D observation.
statement.case_against: The attribution cost is real and I do not think any citation removes it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe quantum wells as the platform that Molenkamp's group then used, Zhang is deceased and cannot be credited, and Bernevig and Hughes are outside every three-name option. Fu and Moore and Balents contributed to the 3D case, and Hasan's group made the first 3D observations, which this configuration leaves unrecognised. A sceptic can also say the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions covers neighbouring ground, and that practical consequences are still modest. I think the 2016 prize recognised topological phases in one-dimensional chains, the quantum Hall effect and phase transitions in two-dimensional films, which is not the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class and does not cover the material discoveries, but the citation should say clearly what is new. Finally, a physicist who cares about who identified the mechanism first must accept that the strict answer is a list of more than three people, and that the cap forces a choice among defensible claimants.

responses.point: Johansson proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing that Hasan's 3D work would otherwise go unrecognised, while accepting that Mele's claim is about equal to Kane's and that the cap, not merit, forces his omission.
responses.response: We agree on the science and on the cost, and I think his own premise points to my slate. If Mele's claim equals Kane's, then leaving him out to include a third strand is exactly the choice that rests on the cap alone. The 3D Z2 invariant came from Fu, Kane and Mele, so the theory pair already carries the 3D idea, and Hasan's ARPES work is the confirmation of a prediction made by that theory. I would rather leave a confirming experiment uncredited than split the founding pair. I do accept his point that the citation should be explicit that the 3D observation is not named, and I propose the citation does not mention the 3D observation as part of the credited discovery. If he can show me that the 3D discovery involved a new idea, not only a confirmation, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Olsson would take Mele over Hasan, because the 3D ARPES work builds on rather than first sights the topological edge state, and asks whether the committee regards the 2016 prize as an obstacle and whether the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit makes any three-person prize defensible.
responses.response: I agree on Mele over Hasan, for the same reason of priority. On the 2016 prize, my answer is that it honours topological phases and phase transitions in low dimensions, in model systems and quantum Hall systems, whereas this configuration recognises a new class of time-reversal-invariant materials and its first realisation; the citation should name the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state so that the distinction is visible. On her second question I do not think the absence of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang makes a three-person prize indefensible, but it does mean the citation must not claim the HgTe prediction as part of the credited theory. Where I would push back is the idea that a later complaint is a reason to pass: every candidate on our shortlist has uncredited contributors, and clocks do too (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto).

responses.point: Lindroth asks the condensed-matter members to say whether omitting Hasan or Mele is the lesser harm, and puts the clean two-name attribution of lattice clocks against B024's credit hole.
responses.response: My answer to her question is that omitting Hasan is the lesser harm, for the reasons I gave Johansson: the experimental confirmation of a 3D prediction is less foundational than the pair who wrote the prediction. I accept that B001 has the cleanest attribution on the list and I regard it as the strongest competing case. My remaining difference is about what is new. The magic-wavelength lattice is an elegant simple mechanism, but its target, the best possible clock, was already the object of the 2005 and 2012 recognitions, and what it added is mainly accuracy. B024 has the larger conceptual step. I would not obstruct B001 on scientific grounds and I would support it above B013 if B024 failed.

responses.point: Pearce says he would shift to B024 as the main prize if the condensed-matter members converge on one trio, and his own configuration pairs clocks with IceCube credited to Halzen alone.
responses.response: I would answer his request directly: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the trio I support, and it follows the theory pair plus the first experiment. As for his two-part prize, I would object to a combination that leaves B024 with a single credited name, because that would credit Molenkamp or Kane alone and sever a founding pair, and I share his own doubts about a one-person credit for a collaboration of hundreds. I do not see a scientific reason to combine unrelated topics, and the chair's own list of disputes suggests the combination would be a compromise rather than a judgment. If the committee goes to a single prize, I would ask him to take B024 on the trio above.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene for its cleaner theory-plus-experiment attribution but would not stand in the way of B024 if the committee finds a defensible trio, and he asks that the 2016 prize be distinguished.
responses.response: I think the trio is defensible and I thank him for saying he would not obstruct it. I hold that B013 is the attractive discovery of the next decade, but my disagreement on maturity stands: the pairing mechanism is open, twist-angle disorder limits reproducibility of the interacting phases, and his own slate drops Bistritzer, so its attribution is not cleaner than ours. His request is reasonable for the citation, and I have worded it around the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state to show what is new compared to 2016.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts omitting Hasan, whose group made the first 3D topological insulator observations, to keep the theory pair intact; a member who weighs experimental discovery above theory priority could reasonably choose the other trio.
Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe proposal, Zhang deceased) and of Fu, Moore and Balents will be seen as too large a cost for a three-name prize.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs on colleagues more than I think, although I regard it as a different class of phenomena.
I rely on memory for dates and priority claims and have not verified them.
How much weight colleagues give to precision measurement against a conceptual advance, which decides the competition between B024 and B001.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent. I have no collaboration with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or any other credited name on the shortlist, and none with the credited names of B001 or B013, my alternatives. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers), which is institutional only. Unchanged from round 1.
